title: The Balance Sheet Equation
context: Review how the balance sheet equation requires total assets to equal total liabilities plus total equity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: An office computer kept in service by an operating business for more than one year is classified as a non-current tangible asset.
An office computer held by a dealer for resale to customers is classified as inventory, a current asset, rather than as a non-current asset.
The same office computer may be a non-current asset for one business and inventory for another, depending on whether it is used or held for sale.
An office computer used by an operating business is classified as inventory because inventory can include any physical equipment a business owns.
Classifying an office computer as a non-current asset depends on management's intention to use it in operations rather than to sell it quickly.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Continued use beyond one year by the business itself makes the office computer a non-current tangible asset.
TRUE — Held for resale rather than use, the office computer counts as inventory under current assets.
TRUE — Intended use versus resale, not physical form, decides whether the office computer is non-current or current.
FALSE — Operational use over the long term makes the office computer a non-current tangible asset, not inventory.
TRUE — Intention to use over the long term is the deciding factor for non-current classification of the office computer.

FALSE — Classification of the office computer depends on whether it is used or held for resale, so identical items can differ across balance sheets.
FALSE — Intended use, not purchase price, drives non-current classification of the office computer.
TRUE — Resale intent places the office computer in inventory, a current asset category.

statements: A profit earned during the year increases the equity reported on the balance sheet, usually by adding to retained earnings.
Depreciation has nothing to do with the wearing out of a fixed asset and is simply an arbitrary bookkeeping entry with no economic meaning.
A loss incurred during the year reduces the equity reported on the balance sheet.
Profit for the year and the change in cash and cash equivalents for the year are two different measures that will not usually be equal.
Cash flow from operating activities reflects cash movements arising from the core trading activities of a business during the period.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Profit for the year raises equity, typically because it is added to retained earnings.
FALSE — Depreciation specifically reflects the loss of value a fixed asset experiences through use over its useful life.
TRUE — A loss for the year lowers retained earnings and therefore reduces total equity.
TRUE — Profit and the net change in cash are distinct measures and typically differ from one another.
TRUE — Operating cash flow captures cash generated or used by a business's day-to-day trading.

title: Cash Flow From Operating Activities
context: Analyze why the statement of profit and loss covers a period rather than a single point in time. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Cash flow from investing activities reflects cash movements arising from buying or selling long-term assets during the period.
Cash flow from financing activities reflects cash movements arising from borrowing, repaying loans, or transactions with owners during the period.
A negative cash flow from investing activities in a given year often signals that a business has been purchasing long-term assets rather than facing financial difficulty.
The net change in cash and cash equivalents for a period is calculated by adding together cash flows from operating, investing and financing activities.
The balance sheet of a bakery shows its assets, equity and liabilities at a single point in time and does not report the value of sales made during the year.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Investing cash flow captures cash spent on, or received from, long-term assets such as equipment.
TRUE — Financing cash flow captures how a business raises and repays funding, including loans and owner transactions.
TRUE — Investing outflows commonly reflect spending on long-term assets rather than an indication of financial trouble.
TRUE — Summing the operating, investing and financing cash flows gives the net change in cash for the period.
TRUE — A balance sheet is a snapshot on one date; sales for the year are reported in the statement of profit and loss, not the balance sheet.

title: Cash Flow From Investing Activities
context: Review how a financial statement typically combines a balance sheet, a statement of profit and loss and a cash flow statement. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Because a bakery draws up its balance sheet at one specific date each year, that document alone cannot reveal how much revenue the business generated over the preceding accounting period.
The balance sheet of a courier firm shows its assets, equity and liabilities at a single point in time and does not report the value of sales made during the year.
The statement of profit and loss prepared by a bakery reports the revenues, costs and resulting profit or loss earned over the accounting period, rather than at a single moment.
A fixed asset that is never depreciated will automatically show a reduced value in the accounts that reflects its true worth after years of use.
Depreciation is a cash expense in the statement of profit and loss that triggers an actual cash payment in the year it is recorded.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Revenue earned over a period is reported in the statement of profit and loss; the balance sheet only reflects the position on its stated date.
TRUE — A balance sheet is a snapshot on one date; sales for the year are reported in the statement of profit and loss, not the balance sheet.
TRUE — Unlike the balance sheet, the statement of profit and loss covers a whole trading period rather than one specific date.
FALSE — Without depreciation, an asset remains at its original cost in the accounts, overstating rather than reflecting its true worth.
FALSE — Depreciation is a non-cash expense; it does not itself trigger a cash payment in the year it is recorded.

title: Reading Financial Statements Cautiously in Practice
context: Analyze how a single year's balance sheet or income statement can be misleading without wider context. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A single year's balance sheet or income statement rarely tells the full story about a business, so the figures are best interpreted alongside additional context rather than read in isolation.

FALSE — A single year's figures rarely tell the full story; wider context and comparison are needed.

TRUE — Multi-year comparison exposes trends hidden within any single year's figures.

TRUE — Comparing balance sheets year on year shows whether assets and financing are growing or shrinking.
